A segment on "Application Domains and System Categories" for an XR course.
VR systems categorized as non-immersive, semi-immersive, or fully immersive based on sensory blocking.

        1. VR immersion = senses blocked from real world, only virtual world.
        2. Categories: non-immersive, semi-immersive, fully immersive (based on market demand/varying immersion degrees).
        3. Non-immersive: specific computer application (not any app), user controls characters/activities while keeping control of physical environment, virtual doesn't directly interact with user.
        4. Non-immersive (psychological): completely takes away attention, user psychologically engaged/may not experience real world, but eyes/ears/organs remain open/physically attached.
        5. Non-immersive examples: gaming (PlayStation, Xbox, World of Warcraft) using consoles/displays and keyboards/mice/handheld controllers.
        6. Semi-immersive: in between, partial immersion, blocks some but not all senses (e.g., eyes blocked, ears/skin exposed).
        7. Semi-immersive examples: 3D environment, user moves through screen/VR box/headset (common), typically no real physical movements, virtual tours (device/web-based).
        8. Semi-immersive traits: most cost-effective and commonly used, most commercial apps because they give partial immersion while leaving user free to sense real world.
        9. Fully immersive: completely blocks ability to sense real world by blocking all senses, user senses only virtual world, feels physically present, sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.
        10. Fully immersive examples: dedicated shooting zones, many devices (helmets, gloves, body connectors, suits), actual movements (running, jumping, etc.) and even blinks detected/translated, user cannot sense anything in real world.
        11. Cost/Rarity: Fully immersive are costliest and commercially rare; semi-immersive and non-immersive are more common.

*   Topic: Understanding Tracking II (Natural Feature Tracking).
    *   Core concepts: Natural feature tracking (NFT) uses features in the environment (points, corners, etc.), descriptors differentiate features, camera pose is estimated by matching descriptors between scene and object, and specific algorithms (SIFT, SURF, BRIEF, BRISK) are used.
    *   Distinctions from other concepts: Fiducial tracking (artificial markers), model-based tracking, SLAM (mapping + localization).

    *   [1] NFT registers camera pose in real-time using features in the natural environment (advanced image processing/computer vision).
    *   [2] Features unique to surroundings (points, corners, line intersections).
    *   [3] Unique descriptors identify/differentiate features.
    *   [4] Pose estimated by matching scene descriptors with object descriptors.
    *   [5] Algorithms: SIFT, SURF, BRIEF, BRISK.

        *   Fact: [1]

Explain how human-eye optics and engineered lens setups are used in VR headsets to create a perceived virtual image while forming a real image on the retina.

    *   [1] Eye structure: Cornea (fixed focal depth), natural lens (variable focal depth), non-planar retina (image surface, converts light to neural pulses).
    *   [2] Eye vs. Lens: Eye has no focal plane (non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces it); artificial lenses have a focal plane.
    *   [3] Media: Eye interior is liquid (light passes through liquid); artificial lenses have air after the lens.
    *   [4] Refractive indices: Air (1.009), cornea (1.376), aqueous fluid (1.336), natural lens (1.413), vitreous fluid (1.337).
    *   [5] Power requirement: Eyeball $\approx$ 24mm diameter, needs $\ge$ 40 diopters to converge parallel rays.
    *   [6] Human eye optics: Cornea ($\approx$ 40D) + Natural lens ($\approx$ 20D) $\approx$ 60D total power for far objects.
    *   [7] VR headset mechanics: Screen close to eyes + convex lens (like reading glasses) focuses screen light on retina.
    *   [8] Distance perception: Screen at focal length of engineered lens $\rightarrow$ enormous virtual image at infinite distance.
    *   [9] Real vs. Virtual: VR shows virtual image, but real image forms on retina (necessary for perception).
